title: Essay Craft: Openings, Endings & Comparison
description: Taking essays further — writing introductions and conclusions, using evidence from texts, and structuring comparative essays.

notes.heading: Introductions: Answer the Question from Sentence One
notes.body: Your introduction has one job above all: show the reader you are answering THIS question, not a question you wish you'd been asked. Two reliable ways to open: (1) Answer the question directly in your first sentence. Question: 'Why is the grandmother an important character in the novel?' Opening: 'The grandmother matters because she is the only character who challenges the family's decision, and her warnings drive the plot towards its climax.' (2) Unpick the key words of the question first. Question: 'How does the writer present courage?' Opening: 'Courage in this story is not physical bravery but the quieter willingness to speak up, and the writer builds this idea through the narrator's smallest choices.' Both approaches keep you focused from the start. After the opening, give one or two sentences of brief context (what the text is, why the topic matters), then state your main idea and signpost the points your body paragraphs will cover — this is where the thesis you learned in Essay Writing & Argumentation does its work. Keep the whole introduction to 3-5 sentences; a long, rambling opening eats the time you need for analysis.

notes.heading: Hooks That Earn Their Place
notes.body: A hook is a first sentence designed to make the reader want to continue. Techniques that work at KS3: a relevant well-known saying given a twist ('They say lightning never strikes twice — the narrator of this story learns otherwise the hard way.'), a short direct question to the reader ('What would you risk to protect a stranger?'), a striking or surprising statement, or a carefully chosen sound pattern like alliteration ('Fear follows the family through every forest scene.'). The golden rule: the hook must be relevant to your actual argument. A clever opening that has nothing to do with your thesis is worse than no hook at all — examiners spot decorative openings instantly. Hooks to avoid: dictionary definitions ('The Oxford Dictionary defines courage as...'), sweeping history-of-the-world claims ('Since the beginning of time, humans have...'), and announcing your own essay ('In this essay I will...'). If you can't think of a genuinely relevant hook, skip it — answering the question directly in sentence one is always a strong opening.

notes.heading: Conclusions: Link Back and Pull Threads Together
notes.body: A conclusion is not a summary dump — it is the moment you prove your essay added up to something. Three moves, in order. (1) Link back to the question using its key words, so the ending clearly answers what was asked: 'Ultimately, the grandmother is important because she embodies the novel's warning that ignored wisdom costs lives.' (2) Reinforce your main points without repeating them — a quick trick is to glance back at your topic sentences and compress them into one or two fresh sentences that show how the points connect, not just that they exist. (3) Stop. Do not introduce new evidence, new quotations, or new arguments in a conclusion; a brilliant new idea here earns nothing because you have no paragraphs left to analyse it. Common mistakes: copying your introduction almost word for word, starting every conclusion with the tired phrase 'In conclusion', and trailing off with a vague sentence like 'So overall it was quite effective.' A missing or weak conclusion makes the whole essay feel unfinished, no matter how good the body was.

notes.heading: The Final Reflection: Leaving the Reader Thinking
notes.body: The strongest conclusions end with a final reflection — one sentence that looks outwards from the text to its wider significance. After linking back and pulling your points together, zoom out: What does this story suggest about people, society, or the reader's own life? Does the ending leave us hopeful or uneasy? Example: 'The rescue at the novel's close offers comfort, but the damage done along the way suggests the writer is less interested in happy endings than in asking what ordinary people owe each other.' Other ways to land the ending: echo a word or image from your introduction (a satisfying 'full circle' effect), answer a question your introduction raised, or adapt a well-known phrase so it fits your argument. Keep the reflection to one or two sentences — it is a parting thought, not a new paragraph of analysis. Pitfall: a reflection that contradicts your thesis or suddenly changes your position. Your conclusion should deepen the reader's sense of your argument, not reopen it.

notes.heading: Choosing Evidence: What Counts and What Works
notes.body: In a literature essay, evidence comes in two forms, and strong essays use both. Direct quotations — the writer's exact words in quotation marks: When Katniss steps forward at the reaping, her cry of 'I volunteer as tribute!' shows her instinct to shield her sister at any cost. References in your own words — retelling a moment briefly to support a point: When Thomas chooses to risk the maze at night for a wounded friend, we see he values loyalty over his own survival. The skill is selection. A quotation earns its place only if it proves the point you are making right now — relevance beats length every time. Short is powerful: one well-chosen word ('growls', 'trembling') gives you more to analyse than a three-line block quote, because you can zoom in on connotations, sound and technique. Before quoting, ask: which exact words carry the meaning? Quote those, and those only. Pitfall: evidence as decoration — dropping in a famous quote because you memorised it, not because it supports your argument. Every quotation should be followed by analysis that unpacks HOW it proves your point.

notes.heading: Embedding Quotations: Grammar, Brackets and Precision
notes.body: Embedding means weaving the writer's words into your own sentence so the result reads as one grammatical whole. You met the basic idea in Essay Writing & Argumentation; here is the precision toolkit. Quote only the key words or phrases: instead of copying a whole sentence, write — The writer likens Harry to a predator when he 'growls' in David's ear. Adjust word endings to fit your grammar using square brackets, which signal to the reader that you altered the original: When Harry 'growl[ed]' the warning, David understood the threat was real. Keep the quotation marks around any words you took directly, even after bracketing them — they are still the writer's words, not yours. Use an ellipsis (...) to skip irrelevant words inside a longer quote: 'the house stood silent... waiting.' Check the join by reading the sentence aloud: if it sounds broken, your embedding is broken. Two pitfalls: tense clashes (mixing the text's past tense with your present analysis without brackets) and 'quote-plonking' — a quotation sitting alone as its own sentence with your writing bolted on either side. Fix plonking by adding a reporting clause: The narrator admits he 'couldn't leave a friend to die', which reveals...

notes.heading: Comparative Essays: Two Texts, One Argument
notes.body: A comparative essay about two fiction texts is not two mini-essays stapled together — it is one argument that keeps both texts in view throughout. Structure it point by point, not text by text: each body paragraph takes one shared point of comparison (a theme, a character type, a narrative technique) and discusses BOTH texts on that point before moving on. Even when a point is mostly about one text, name the other briefly so the thread never drops. Fuel the comparison with connectives: similarity — 'similarly', 'likewise', 'equally', 'in the same way'; contrast — 'whereas', 'however', 'in contrast', 'while'. Example move: 'Both novels trap their young heroes inside brutal systems; however, where one tells the story through a first-person 'I' that puts us inside the heroine's fear, the other uses a third-person narrator who watches the hero from a distance — yet both perspectives make us care whether he survives.' Compare things worth comparing: themes, characters, narrative voice, setting, structure, language techniques — not surface trivia like chapter counts. Introduction: name both texts and your comparative thesis. Conclusion: link back to the question and mention both texts. The block method (all of Text A, then all of Text B) almost always produces description, not comparison — avoid it.

flashcards.definition: An opening sentence that grabs the reader's attention — a relevant saying, question, or striking statement. It must connect to your argument.
flashcards.example: 'What would you risk to protect a stranger?' — opening an essay about self-sacrifice in a novel.

flashcards.definition: Answering the essay question in your very first sentence, then building the rest of the introduction on it.
flashcards.example: Q: 'Why is the grandmother important?' A: 'The grandmother matters because her warnings drive the plot towards its climax.'

flashcards.definition: The important words in the essay title that you explore in your opening and reuse in your conclusion to stay focused.
flashcards.example: For 'How does the writer present courage?', unpack 'courage' first: what kind of courage does the text actually show?

flashcards.definition: A brief sentence or two in the introduction showing why the topic or text matters — placed between the hook and the main idea.
flashcards.example: 'Stories about survival ask what people become when the rules of ordinary life fall away.'

flashcards.definition: Reusing the key words of the essay question in your conclusion so your ending clearly answers what was asked.
flashcards.example: Q about why a character is 'important' → conclusion: 'Ultimately, Jack is important because he embodies the novel's warning about power.'

flashcards.definition: A closing thought that looks outwards from the text to its wider significance — one or two sentences, never new analysis.
flashcards.example: 'The hopeful ending leaves us asking what ordinary people owe each other when systems fail.'

flashcards.definition: Quoting only the key words or phrases that carry the meaning, rather than whole sentences — gives you more to analyse.
flashcards.example: Quote just 'growls' and analyse its animal connotations, instead of copying three full lines.

flashcards.definition: Brackets showing you changed a word ending (e.g. tense) so the quotation fits your sentence grammatically.
flashcards.example: When Harry 'growl[ed]' the warning, David understood the threat was real.

flashcards.definition: Referring to an event from the text in your own words to support a point — an alternative to direct quotation.
flashcards.example: 'When Thomas risks the maze at night for a wounded friend, we see he values loyalty over survival.'

flashcards.definition: Linking words that signal similarity (similarly, likewise, equally) or contrast (whereas, however, in contrast) between texts.
flashcards.example: 'Both heroes defy their rulers; however, one acts from duty whereas the other acts from anger.'

flashcards.definition: Structuring a comparative essay so each paragraph covers one shared point and discusses BOTH texts on it — the strongest method.
flashcards.example: Paragraph on narrative voice: Text A's first person vs Text B's third person, in the same paragraph.

flashcards.definition: Writing everything about Text A, then everything about Text B — weak for comparison because the texts never meet.
flashcards.example: Three paragraphs on one novel followed by three on the other = two mini-essays, not a comparison.

questions.stem: What is the most important job of an essay introduction?
choices: To summarise the whole plot of the text
To list every technique the writer uses
To show you are answering the specific question set, and state your main idea
To include as many quotations as possible
questions.explanation: An introduction must answer the actual question from sentence one and present your main idea. Plot summary and technique-listing belong nowhere in an introduction, and quotations are saved for body paragraphs where they can be analysed.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest conclusion move for the question 'Why is the grandmother an important character?'
choices: 'Ultimately, the grandmother is important because her ignored warnings drive the novel towards its tragic climax.'
'In conclusion, this essay has written about the grandmother.'
'Another interesting character is the narrator's brother, who also deserves attention.'
'The grandmother appears in chapters one, four, seven and nine.'
questions.explanation: The first option links back to the question's key words ('important character') and compresses the essay's argument into a fresh sentence. The second announces rather than concludes, the third introduces a new topic, and the fourth is plot summary, not argument.

questions.stem: Which connective signals SIMILARITY between two texts?
choices: Whereas
Similarly
However
In contrast
questions.explanation: 'Similarly' (like 'likewise' and 'equally') tells the reader the two texts do the same thing. 'Whereas', 'however' and 'in contrast' all signal difference — useful in the same essay, but for the opposite move.

questions.stem: Why is quoting a single word like 'growls' often better than quoting a whole three-line sentence?
choices: It saves time and examiners reward brevity
Long quotations are against the rules
Single words never need quotation marks
It lets you zoom in on connotations, sound and technique — more analysis per word
questions.explanation: A short, selective quotation gives you something precise to analyse: the animal connotations of 'growls', its harsh sound, the writer's choice. Long block quotes dilute analysis. Length isn't against the rules, and quoted words always need quotation marks however short they are.

questions.stem: Even after you change a quotation's tense with square brackets, you must still:
choices: Keep quotation marks around the words taken directly from the text
Underline the changed words
Name the chapter number
Put the whole sentence in italics
questions.explanation: Bracketed words are still the writer's words — 'growl[ed]' was 'growls' in the text — so the quotation marks stay. The brackets only flag that you adjusted the ending to fit your sentence's grammar.

questions.stem: Question: 'How does the writer present fear in the opening chapter?' Which first sentence answers it most directly?
choices: 'Fear is an emotion experienced by all humans throughout history.'
'The opening chapter presents fear as contagious, spreading from one character's panic to the whole group through fragmented sentences and sensory detail.'
'In this essay I will discuss how the writer presents fear.'
'The novel was published in 2015 and won several awards.'
questions.explanation: The second sentence takes a stance on HOW fear is presented (as contagious) and previews the analysis (fragmented sentences, sensory detail). The first is a sweeping generalisation, the third announces rather than argues, and the fourth is irrelevant biographical trivia.

questions.stem: Your point: 'The narrator is unreliable.' Which evidence best supports it?
choices: The moment the narrator admits 'I may have invented most of what happened that night'
A description of the weather in chapter two
The fact that the novel is written in the first person
The author's biography, which mentions a difficult childhood
questions.explanation: The narrator's own admission directly proves the point — relevance is the test every quotation must pass. First-person narration alone doesn't make a narrator unreliable, weather is off-point, and the author's life is context, not textual evidence for this claim.

questions.stem: In a comparative essay, why should each body paragraph mention BOTH texts?
choices: Because examiners count how many times each title appears
It makes the essay longer
Because the second text is usually more important
Because comparison is the argument — dropping one text turns the paragraph into isolated description
questions.explanation: The comparison IS the point: each paragraph takes one shared idea and weighs both texts against it. If a paragraph discusses only one text, you've built two mini-essays that never meet. Name-dropping titles without comparing earns nothing.

questions.stem: Which sentence embeds a quotation most skilfully?
choices: 'The character is threatening. 'He growls the warning in her ear.' This shows danger.'
'The writer signals danger: 'He growls the warning in her ear and steps closer, his shadow falling across the door and the window and the floor.''
'The character's threat feels animal-like when he 'growls' the warning, the verb stripping away his humanity.'
''Growls.' This word is about the character being threatening.'
questions.explanation: The third option selects just the key word, weaves it into a grammatical sentence, and follows it with analysis of its connotations. The first 'plonks' a standalone quote, the second quotes far more than it needs, and the fourth starts the sentence with a naked quotation.

questions.stem: A quick way to build the 'reinforce your main points' part of a conclusion is to:
choices: Copy your introduction and change a few words
Repeat your best quotation so the reader remembers it
Look back at your topic sentences and compress them into one or two fresh connecting sentences
List every paragraph in order: 'Firstly I said... secondly I said...'
questions.explanation: Your topic sentences already hold your argument's skeleton — the conclusion compresses them into fresh sentences that show how the points connect. Copying the introduction is lazy repetition, repeating a quotation adds nothing, and a mechanical list summarises rather than synthesises.

questions.stem: Which sentence makes a genuine comparison rather than two separate observations?
choices: 'Both novels trap their heroes inside brutal systems; however, where one uses a first-person voice that puts us inside the heroine's fear, the other watches its hero from a third-person distance.'
'Novel A is written in the first person. Novel B is written in the third person.'
'Novel A is exciting and Novel B is also exciting.'
'The heroine of Novel A is brave, and there is also a hero in Novel B.'
questions.explanation: The first option names the shared point (brutal systems), uses 'however' and 'where' to weigh the texts against each other, and shows the effect of each choice. The others place the texts side by side without analysing the relationship between them.

questions.stem: The text says: 'She runs to the window and freezes.' Your essay is in past tense. Which embedded version is grammatically correct?
choices: She 'runs to the window and freezes' showed her terror.
She 'ran to the window and froze', showing her terror. (no brackets needed)
When she 'r[an] to the window and fr[oze]', her terror was unmistakable.
Terror: 'She runs to the window and freezes.'
questions.explanation: Square brackets let you adjust the verb endings ('runs' → 'r[an]', 'freezes' → 'fr[oze]') so the quote fits your past-tense sentence, while quotation marks show the words came from the text. The first option keeps a tense clash, the second changes the words without flagging it, and the fourth plonks the quote.

choices: A paragraph summarising Text A's plot, followed by a paragraph summarising Text B's plot
A paragraph on setting that argues Text A's city isolates its hero whereas Text B's island forces rivals together — then links both settings to the theme of survival
A paragraph listing every difference between the two books, from page count to publication date
A paragraph praising Text A and explaining why Text B is worse
questions.explanation: The second option takes one shared point (setting), weighs both texts on it in the same paragraph, and connects the comparison to a theme — the integrated method. Plot-by-plot is the weak block method, trivia lists aren't analysis, and ranking the texts isn't comparing them.

questions.stem: Which hook is most appropriate for an essay arguing that a novel's hero succeeds through teamwork rather than individual strength?
choices: 'The Oxford Dictionary defines a hero as a person admired for brave acts.'
'Since the dawn of time, humans have told stories about heroes.'
'This essay will argue that the hero succeeds through teamwork.'
'No one climbs a mountain alone — and this novel's hero is no exception, owing every victory to the allies around him.'
questions.explanation: The fourth option grabs attention AND feeds directly into the argument (teamwork over solo strength). Dictionary definitions and 'dawn of time' openings are generic filler that could sit on any essay, and announcing your essay is a plan statement, not a hook.

questions.stem: A student ends their essay: 'In conclusion, I have shown the main points. Also, the writer uses pathetic fallacy in chapter eleven, which I forgot to mention earlier.' What is the main problem?
choices: The conclusion introduces a brand-new point (pathetic fallacy) with no paragraph left to analyse it
Conclusions must never mention techniques
The conclusion is too long
The phrase 'In conclusion' is grammatically incorrect
questions.explanation: New evidence in a conclusion earns nothing because there is no space to analyse how it supports the thesis — the point should have been a body paragraph or left out. Techniques are fine to reference in a conclusion if already argued, and 'In conclusion' is tired but grammatical.
